title: God’s Faithfulness and Israel’s Unfaithfulness
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: God Desires Heart Faithfulness
subpoints: God values mercy and knowledge of Him over empty sacrifices
True religion involves a changed heart, not just outward conformity
Faithfulness and obedience to God's word are inseparable

outline.title: Israel's Response: Treachery and Wickedness
subpoints: Israel transgressed the covenant like Adam
The term 'treacherous' indicates a faithless heart
Outward rituals did not mask internal rebellion

outline.title: Interpreting 'Like Adam' vs. 'At Adam'
subpoints: Textual evidence supports 'like Adam' (simile) over 'at Adam' (location)
No ancient version supports the emendation to a place name
The comparison highlights the nature of the covenant break

outline.title: The Parallel with Adam's Sin
subpoints: Adam broke the Covenant of Works through a desire for autonomy
Israel similarly sought to be their own boss rather than God's people
Romans 5:18 illustrates the corporate nature of Adam's offense

outline.title: Evidence of Israel's Treachery
subpoints: Violence and murder in Gilead and Shechem
Priests acting as robbers and committing lewdness
The 'harvest' of judgment appointed for Judah and Ephraim

summary:
In this sermon, Pastor Tito Lyro explores the theme of God's desire for genuine covenant faithfulness from the heart, contrasting it with Israel's outward religious performance. Drawing from Hosea 6:6, the message emphasizes that God values mercy and the knowledge of Himself more than burnt offerings, challenging the modern notion that 'religion' is a negative term. Instead, true religion is defined by a heart transformed by God, leading to both faithfulness and obedience to His word.

The sermon addresses the interpretation of Hosea 6:7, arguing against the common view that 'Adam' refers to a location. By examining the Hebrew text and ancient versions, it is concluded that the phrase 'like Adam' is the more faithful reading. This interpretation highlights a profound theological parallel: just as Adam broke the Covenant of Works by seeking autonomy and rejecting God's authority, Israel broke the Mosaic Covenant by acting treacherously and attempting to be their own masters.

The message concludes by detailing the evidence of Israel's treachery, including violence in Gilead and Shechem and the moral corruption of the priesthood. These actions demonstrate that Israel's sacrifices were empty because their hearts remained unfaithful. The sermon calls the congregation to examine their own hearts, ensuring that their worship and service stem from a sincere, God-shaped faithfulness rather than empty conformity.
